title: Gluing and filtered-colimit stability for simplicial weak equivalences
statement:
Use simplicial sets, monomorphisms and weak homotopy equivalences of [lem-coef-kan-quillen-model-right-proper-core]. Let $A_i\xrightarrow{u_i}B_i$, $A_i\xrightarrow{v_i}C_i$ for $i=0,1$ be two spans of small simplicial sets, with $u_0,u_1$ monomorphisms. Let $(a,b,c)$ be a commuting map from the first span to the second, all three components weak homotopy equivalences. Then the induced map $B_0\amalg_{A_0}C_0\to B_1\amalg_{A_1}C_1$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

Let $I$ be a small nonempty partially ordered set in which every finite subset has an upper bound, viewed as a category with one arrow $i\to j$ exactly when $i\leq j$. For diagrams $X,Y:I\to\mathrm{sSet}$ and a natural transformation $f:X\to Y$ whose components are weak homotopy equivalences, the map $\operatorname{colim}_I X\to\operatorname{colim}_I Y$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. These colimits and pushouts are formed degreewise in sets; the transition maps need not be monomorphisms.

source.place: Lemma 5.2.6 (cube lemma), printed pp. 126-127, specialized to simplicial sets; filtered-colimit assertion: HTT Section A.2.7, Kan-model discussion following Example A.2.7.3 and Proposition A.2.6.15, condition (1), with Definition A.2.6.12(3); also used explicitly in HTT Proposition 2.2.2.7. No Stacks tag states these simplicial homotopy assertions.

proof.text: Let $J$ have three objects $c,a,b$ and only the two nonidentity arrows $a\to c$ and $a\to b$. Give them degrees $0,1,2$, respectively; let $J^-$ contain $a\to c$ and $J^+$ contain $a\to b$, together with all identities. Every arrow has the required unique inverse-then-direct factorization, so the Reedy-model theorem applies. The latching objects of a span $D=(C\leftarrow A\to B)$ are $L_cD=L_aD=\varnothing$ and $L_bD=A$; the matching objects are $M_cD=M_bD=*$ and $M_aD=C$. In Kan–Quillen simplicial sets every object is cofibrant: its initial map from $\varnothing$ is degreewise injective. Thus the Reedy cofibrancy conditions on $D$ are exactly the monomorphism condition on $A\to B$. Both given spans $D_0,D_1$ are Reedy cofibrant, and $f=(c,a,b):D_0\to D_1$ is a Reedy weak equivalence because Reedy weak equivalences are objectwise.

source.place: Lemma 5.2.6, printed pp. 126–127: the mixed Reedy structure on the span

proof.text: Let $P:\mathrm{sSet}^J\to\mathrm{sSet}$ send a diagram to its ordinary colimit. It is left adjoint to the constant diagram functor: a map from $PD$ to $T$ is exactly a family of maps $D_j\to T$ commuting with both span arrows, by the colimit universal property. For any Kan–Quillen fibration $q:E\to T$, the relative matching maps of the constant transformation $\operatorname{const}(q)$ are $q$ at $c,b$ and the isomorphism $E\to T\times_T E$ at $a$. The latter is a fibration: every lifting square against a trivial cofibration fills using the inverse isomorphism. Hence $\operatorname{const}(q)$ is a Reedy fibration. If $j:D\to D'$ is a Reedy trivial cofibration, a lifting square from $Pj$ to $q$ is, by the displayed adjunction, exactly a square from $j$ to $\operatorname{const}(q)$. The Reedy lifting axiom fills it, and adjunction returns a lift of the original square. Thus $Pj$ has the left lifting property against every Kan–Quillen fibration, so the Kan–Quillen weak factorization system identifies $Pj$ as a trivial cofibration. This proves the needed preservation assertion directly, without invoking a derived-adjunction or localization theorem.

source.place: Proof of Lemma 5.2.6, printed p. 127: constant diagrams preserve fibrations, and the colimit adjunction transfers lifts

proof.text: Apply the cofibrant half of the split-factorization statement to the Reedy weak equivalence $f:D_0\to D_1$. Its model hypotheses hold for the Reedy model structure: weak equivalences are retract closed, and the cofibrations and fibrations are retract closed as lifting classes by the cited lifting-class-closure statement. We obtain $Z$, a cofibration $i:D_0\to Z$, a trivial fibration $p:Z\to D_1$, and a cofibration $s:D_1\to Z$, with $pi=f$ and $ps=1$. Reedy two-out-of-three shows that both $i$ and $s$ are weak equivalences, since $p,f$ and $1$ are; hence they are Reedy trivial cofibrations. Step 2 gives weak equivalences $Pi$ and $Ps$. The identity $(Pp)(Ps)=1$ and Kan–Quillen two-out-of-three imply $Pp$ is a weak equivalence; composition gives $Pf=(Pp)(Pi)$ a weak equivalence. The universal property identifies $PD_i$ with $C_i\amalg_{A_i}B_i$. Swapping the pushout legs gives the canonical symmetry isomorphism with $B_i\amalg_{A_i}C_i$; its comparison squares commute since both composites restrict to the prescribed maps $b,c$ on the legs. Thus $Pf$ is exactly the induced map in the first clause, up to these isomorphisms, and proves that clause.

source.place: Proof of Ken Brown’s Lemma 1.1.12, printed pp. 6–7, applied to the colimit functor from the mixed Reedy span model; Lemma 5.2.6, printed pp. 126–127

proof.text: For the second clause, the assumed nonempty poset $I$ is filtered: an upper bound of $\{i,j\}$ gives the required common target, and parallel arrows are equal and thus equalized by an identity. We will use the following finite-data calculation, also for the sequential poset $\mathbf N$. A degreewise colimit has elements represented by $(i,x)$, and $(i,x)$ and $(j,y)$ represent the same element precisely when their images agree at some common upper bound. The latter relation is an equivalence relation (transitivity uses a common upper bound of two witnesses), and this quotient has the cocone universal property. Any finite collection of representatives and equalities therefore occurs at one common stage. A map $\Delta^r\to Z$ is specified by the image of its identity $r$-simplex, all other images being its simplicial operators. A map from a boundary or horn is specified by its finitely many face simplices, with the equalities on their pairwise face intersections; intersections are themselves faces, and degeneracies introduce no additional choices. Consequently maps from $\Delta^r$, $\partial\Delta^r$, or $\Lambda_t^r$ into a directed degreewise colimit descend to one stage, and equality of two such maps holds at some later common stage. The empty boundary $\partial\Delta^0$ has the unique map and requires no data. This argument also descends a commuting square involving these shapes: descend its two maps, then pass to a later stage where its finitely many commutativity equations hold.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.8.1 (00UV), finite horn data; explicit representative/equality calculation supplied here. Filteredness: Stacks Tag 002V, categories.tex, definition-directed.

proof.text: Construct a factorization for each arbitrary simplicial map $g:U\to V$ as follows. Set $U^{(0)}=U$, with $g^{(0)}=g$. Given $g^{(m)}:U^{(m)}\to V$, for each $r\geq1$ and $0\leq t\leq r$ let $S_{r,t}^{(m)}$ be the set of pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ with $\alpha:\Lambda_t^r\to U^{(m)}$, $\beta:\Delta^r\to V$, and $g^{(m)}\alpha=\beta|_{\Lambda_t^r}$. Form $U^{(m+1)}$ by the pushout of $\coprod_{r,t}\coprod_{S_{r,t}^{(m)}}\Lambda_t^r\to U^{(m)}$ along $\coprod_{r,t}\coprod_{S_{r,t}^{(m)}}\Lambda_t^r\hookrightarrow\coprod_{r,t}\coprod_{S_{r,t}^{(m)}}\Delta^r$. The top map evaluates $\alpha$ on each summand, and the maps $\beta$ extend $g^{(m)}$ to $g^{(m+1)}$. Put $Q(g)=\operatorname{colim}_{m\in\mathbf N}U^{(m)}$. The resulting $j_g:U\to Q(g)$ is a countable composite of pushouts of coproducts of horn inclusions, hence a trivial cofibration by the horn-cell characterization in the Kan–Quillen statement (a cell map is its own retract). Let $p_g:Q(g)\to V$ be induced by the $g^{(m)}$. A horn square against $p_g$ descends by Step 4 to some $U^{(m)}$ with its commutativity equation valid there; the corresponding simplex attached at $m+1$ fills it. Thus $p_g$ is a Kan fibration and $g=p_gj_g$. A commuting square from $g$ to $g'$ sends $(\alpha,\beta)$ to its pair of composites. It therefore induces the maps of the displayed pushouts at each stage and then of their sequential colimits. Identities and compositions agree on the old object and every attached simplex, so agree by the pushout and colimit universal properties. This makes $Q,j,p$ functorial, not just a collection of unrelated factorizations. All displayed coproducts have small indexing sets because all objects and hom-sets are small.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.8.1 (00UV), recursive simultaneous horn-attachment construction and the finite-stage filler proof.

proof.text: For the diagram $f_i:X_i\to Y_i$, write $U_i^{(m)}$, $S_{r,t,i}^{(m)}$ for this construction. We check that its canonical comparison with the construction on $\bar f=\operatorname{colim}_I f_i$ is an isomorphism at every $m$. At $m=0$ this is the definition. Assuming it at $m$, Step 4 says that each pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ defining a horn square for $\operatorname{colim}_I U_i^{(m)}\to\operatorname{colim}_I Y_i$ descends with its equation to some $i$, and two such pairs agree precisely after a common later stage. Hence $\operatorname{colim}_I S_{r,t,i}^{(m)}\cong S_{r,t}^{(m)}$ for the construction on $\bar f$. For a fixed simplicial shape $K$, the canonical map $\operatorname{colim}_I\coprod_{s\in S_i}K\to\coprod_{s\in\operatorname{colim}_I S_i}K$ is degreewise bijective: an element is a pair $(s,k)$, its $K$-coordinate never changes, and equality of its $s$-coordinate is eventual equality. The further coproduct over fixed labels $(r,t)$ also commutes with the colimit, since transitions preserve these labels. Finally colimits commute with these pushouts: a map from either iterated construction to $T$ is the same compatible family of maps on the old objects and attached simplices agreeing on each attaching horn. This proves the induction step by the pushout universal property. Maps from $\operatorname{colim}_I\operatorname{colim}_m U_i^{(m)}$ and from $\operatorname{colim}_m\operatorname{colim}_I U_i^{(m)}$ to $T$ are likewise the same family compatible in both indices. Thus the canonical map $\theta:\operatorname{colim}_I Q(f_i)\xrightarrow{\sim}Q(\bar f)$ is an isomorphism. Every comparison above agrees on each original simplex and every attached simplex, so $\theta\,(\operatorname{colim}_I j_{f_i})=j_{\bar f}$ and $p_{\bar f}\theta=\operatorname{colim}_I p_{f_i}$.

source.place: Proposition 3.1.8.1 (00UV), filtered-colimit preservation: its omitted verification expanded as the induction on attachment stages and the two explicit cocone calculations.

proof.text: Each $j_{f_i}$ is a weak equivalence by Step 5. Since $f_i=p_{f_i}j_{f_i}$ is a weak equivalence by hypothesis, two-out-of-three in the Kan–Quillen model makes $p_{f_i}$ a weak equivalence. It is already a fibration, so is a trivial fibration. Let $\bar p=\operatorname{colim}_I p_{f_i}$. A square from $\partial\Delta^r\hookrightarrow\Delta^r$ to $\bar p$ descends by Step 4 to a square against some $p_{f_i}$; the filler there composes to a filler for the original square. This includes $r=0$, where the upper map is empty and only the lower vertex needs a representative. The boundary-lifting characterization in the Kan–Quillen statement implies that $\bar p$ is a trivial fibration, hence a weak equivalence. Step 6 identifies $\bar j=\operatorname{colim}_I j_{f_i}$, via $\theta$, with the horn-cell map $j_{\bar f}$ of Step 5, so $\bar j$ is a weak equivalence as well. Isomorphisms are weak equivalences because realization carries an inverse to an inverse, giving inverse maps on components and all based homotopy groups. Finally $\bar f=\bar p\bar j$: both composites agree after every $X_i\to\operatorname{colim}_I X_i$ by $p_{f_i}j_{f_i}=f_i$, so the colimit universal property gives equality. Two-out-of-three now makes $\bar f$ a weak equivalence, proving precisely the canonical map of the second clause, without any injectivity assumption on the transitions.

source.place: Proposition 3.2.8.3 (00XE), reduction to trivial Kan fibrations; boundary lifting and two-out-of-three supplied by the cited Kan–Quillen model.
